newsitem.title: USA: Best things in life can indeed be free.
newsitem.headline: Best things in life can indeed be free.

text.p: Who said there's no such thing as a free lunch? Not Bob and Linda Kalian, who believe that not only are there free lunches, there are free cruises, free computer products and, no joke, free dirt.

"I was absolultely blown away last Saturday. I got 100 free computer disks and a mouse at one store, and at another store I got a free surge-protector," said Bob Kalian, from his business office in the New York City suburb of Hartsdale, N.Y.

"There's a battle going on between computer retailers. Invariably the consumer benefits. They're offering irresistible offers that become totally free with rebates," he said. "You have to lay down money but you get 100 percent of the money back."

The Kalians, who run a printing company and mail order concern, have put their years of freebie collecting into a book, "The Best Free Things in America," published by their own company, Roblin Press ($8.95).
Companies spend millions of dollars on advertising and good will to get and keep customers, and savvy consumers have learned that there's a lot out there free for the asking.
Take long distance telephone giants MCI, AT&T and Sprint. Bob said a consumer could get a $100 check from ATT, authorising the carrier to switch the consumer's long distance service.
"But there's no obligation to stay with that particular carrier," he said. The $100 is yours.
The most unusual freebie the Kalians ever received was the forementioned dirt, needed to fill a huge hole left after construction of their new home six years ago.

"There was a big hole that would have cost $2,000 to $3,000 to fill," said Bob, who went to a local construction site and asked the engineers there what they planned to do with all the land fill they had removed. For free, they hauled trucks full of dirt to fill in the Kalians' yard.

The Kalians' involvement in the world of freebies started years ago when Linda, an avid recipe collector, started getting free offers and coupons from food companies. "Consumer companies like Hunts, Mullers and Ronzoni want to get you as a loyal customer," Linda said.
"Bob got jealous," she said, "and thought there must be other things out there."
Over the years, the Kalians have saved thousands of dollars, or "$2,000 to $3,000 a year, conservatively," Bob said.
Last year, they got a cruise -- free, a result of overbooking.
"Let it be known that you have flexability and can be bumped if need be," he said. The reward for being a victim of airline or cruiseline overbooking is almost always a free ticket.
"They (cruise ships) are also looking for people who can provide a service" such as giving a lecture on a particular speciality, in exchange for a free trip, Linda said.
The Kalians "have devoted our lives to this, but it doesn't require that much time," Linda said.

Today, Bob keeps on top of freebies by keeping a pad and pencil by his side, especially when watching television. He jots down toll-free telephone numbers for vacation spots or consumer products and information. Later, he will call the numbers and get whatever they're offering, be it posters, coupons or product samples.
But the Kalians feel it's important to keep the freebie life in perspective. It's a way of having fun, rather than a money-making exercise, they say.

But the freebie life also has some very serious, tangible benefits. The Kalians' two sons were able to get virtually free college educations due to a combination of scholarships, grants and work study programmes.
Their parents contributed about $5,000 a year for room and board.
"There are billions of dollars out there (for college educations), but you have to find the resources and toll free numbers. It takes a bit of work but the reward is worth it," Bob said.
The first step is always the college's financial aid office. Other resources include the public library and government agencies, such as Sallie Mae.
